design_detail: Memorial lecture (the sixth Thomas James Okey Memorial Lecture, published in Addiction) in which the principal investigator looks back 20 years on her follow-up of US Army enlisted men who left Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8–12 months and 3 years after return, with a matched civilian comparison group, and reviews six other studies of recovery from heroin addiction (plus her own earlier St Louis study). The figures are reproduced from the study's earlier reports; methods are given only in outline: no total sample size in the text, no definition of addiction beyond self-report checked against frequency, duration and withdrawal, no confidence intervals.
can_establish: The principal investigator's own account of what her Vietnam follow-up found: how common narcotic use and self-reported addiction were in Vietnam in 1970–71, how few men addicted there were addicted again after return (5% in the first year, 12% at any time in 3 years), that recovery mostly happened without treatment and despite some renewed use, and what she argues this means for views of heroin addiction.
cannot_establish: The study's methods and precision (sample sizes, response by group, the definition of addiction and the weighting are given only in outline); whether the results apply outside Vietnam's conditions, which the author herself calls unprecedented; or that treatment does not work (the few men treated were, by the author's own reading, those who could not stop on their own).

sample.recruitment: Two samples of US Army enlisted men who left Vietnam in September 1971, the first month departure urine screening ran throughout the country: one drawn from a Department of Defense tape of the active-duty roster (22,000 names; the true number of September returnees was later estimated at 13,280), and one from the Surgeon General's records of men whose departure urine was positive, used to over-sample men who used heroin (over 600 men who used narcotics in Vietnam were interviewed) and weighted back to their share of the population. A comparison sample of draft-eligible civilians who did not serve, matched on age, region and education at service entry, was drawn from Selective Service records (pp. 1042–1043).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Army enlisted men below officer level, on Department of Defense advice that most heroin use was in this group; men whose military records showed they never served in Vietnam or left before September were dropped (p. 1043).
sample.demographics: Men. Draftees were drafted at 18, typically reached Vietnam at about 19 and were discharged at 20 or 21; volunteers had 3-year terms (p. 1043). Race, education and other characteristics are not reported in the lecture.
sample.attrition: Interview completion 96% at 8–12 months after return; 94% of those were re-interviewed 3 years after departure (p. 1042).
sample.selection_effects: One cohort of young enlisted men from a single month's departures, during the Army's 'stand-down' (p. 1043). Heroin in Vietnam was cheap (about $6 a day for a man who was addicted), pure and did not have to be injected, and more than 80% of men were offered it, usually within a week of arrival (pp. 1044, 1048). The author says there had never been a time when so many young men were addicted to opiates in the absence of the usual risk factors, and that few of them would have become addicted had they stayed in the US (p. 1051).

exposure.measurement: Interview self-report: 20% said they had felt strung out or addicted to narcotics in Vietnam; the claims were checked against reported frequency and length of use and withdrawal symptoms and accepted (p. 1044). Departure urine screen (FRAT, positives re-tested by gas chromatography; p. 1042): almost 11% of enlisted men positive (p. 1044). Honesty checks: 97% of men whose military record showed narcotic use reported it, and urine collected after each interview showed no more current use than the men had reported (p. 1042).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not quantified. Tours in Vietnam lasted about a year (p. 1043).
exposure.polysubstance: Common. Close to 80% used marijuana in Vietnam (p. 1044). After return, men who used heroin also used many other drugs (more than 80% amphetamines, more than 70% barbiturates, almost all marijuana), and more than half of those addicted to heroin named alcohol or marijuana as their main drug (p. 1046). In Vietnam, narcotic use and drinking were inversely related (Figure 2, p. 1045).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; urine was collected at the end of each interview (p. 1042).

comparison.controls: Draft-eligible civilian men who did not serve, matched to the veterans on age, region and education at service entry (p. 1042); and, for relapse, young men treated at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington and followed 6 months after release (122 NARA patients; Stephens & Cottrell, 1972; p. 1045, Figure 4 p. 1047).
comparison.matching: Civilians matched on age, region and education at entry. The civilian comparison is used only for the statement that marijuana and narcotic use were distinctively greater in the veterans (pp. 1044–1045); no civilian figures are given.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Pre-service deviance (fighting, truancy, drunkenness, arrest, school expulsion) and pre-service drug use were measured retrospectively at interview and predicted narcotic use in Vietnam (Figures 3 and 7); no pre-service clinical or biological measures.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Civilian controls' drug use is not reported in the lecture.

outcomes.instruments: Structured interviews by the National Opinion Research Center at 8–12 months and 3 years after return; urine tests at the end of each interview; military and Veterans Administration records (pp. 1042–1043).
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-report checked against military records (97% concordance among men with recorded narcotic use) and post-interview urine tests (p. 1042).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Addiction' is not defined in the lecture beyond self-report checked against frequency, duration and withdrawal (p. 1044). 'Re-addiction', 'relapse' (Figure 5: relapse to drug use) and the use categories of Figure 4 (no use, light use, heavy use, addiction) are not defined.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages only, without confidence intervals or denominators. In Vietnam: 45% tried narcotics, 34% heroin, 38% opium; close to 80% used marijuana; 20% reported addiction; almost 11% urine-positive at departure (p. 1044). After return, among men addicted in Vietnam: 5% addicted in the first year and 12% at any time in 3 years (p. 1045); 6% re-addicted 'overall', and half of the men who used heroin regularly re-addicted (p. 1046). In the 8–10 months after return, about 2% of men first addicted in Vietnam in the general sample (n=90) and about 7% in the drug-positive sample (n=341) were addicted, against about 70% of 122 NARA patients 6 months after release (read from Figure 4, p. 1047). Men treated after return: two-thirds relapsed by the time of interview (p. 1046).
analysis.covariates: Not described. Holding pre-service behaviour problems and number of drug types constant is mentioned for the comparison of heroin with amphetamines and barbiturates (p. 1046), and taking pre-service history into account for combat (p. 1049).
analysis.selective_reporting: A retrospective lecture by the principal investigator: denominators, time frames and weighting are rarely given, and several figures in the text differ from the lecture's own graphs (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Narcotic use and self-reported addiction were common among US Army enlisted men in Vietnam in 1970–71 (45% tried narcotics; 20% reported addiction). After return, few men who had been addicted in Vietnam were addicted again (5% in the first year; 12% at any time in 3 years), usually briefly, although many used narcotics again; few were treated, and those treated relapsed at about the rate of civilian patients (two-thirds).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The author concludes the results were both correct and not unique (p. 1051), that heroin is not an exceptional drug, that the typical patient for whom heroin treatment programmes are designed is a mythological creature (p. 1051), and that addiction tends to remit quickly even without treatment (pp. 1050–1051). She qualifies this herself: so many young men had never before been addicted to opiates without the usual risk factors, and few would have become addicted had they stayed in the US (p. 1051); and vulnerability to re-addiction among men who used again may be biological (p. 1053). The 'not unique' claim rests on six small or indirect studies (an ethnography of 50 people, 22 men in her St Louis study, two youth surveys, Winick's register analysis and the ECA, most of whose cases did not involve heroin), not on another population exposed as the veterans were. The answer to the setting-change explanation rests on the men who used heroin again in the US, most of whom were not re-addicted; it is not a direct test of a setting effect. Treated men relapsing as often as civilian patients is read as evidence that treated cases are those who cannot stop alone, not as a measure of what treatment adds.

timeline.event: Winick's analysis of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics records and the New York Narcotics Register: names tended to drop off at ages 35 to 40, or after 5 years; with no interviews he could not show that people had stopped rather than moved, died or avoided arrest (as described here, p. 1049).

Robins and Murphy's study of 235 Black men born in St Louis: of 22 who reported heroin addiction, four had used any heroin in the year before interview at 31–35, and four had ever been treated (as described here, pp. 1042, 1050).
Robins, Davis and Nurco, 'How permanent was Vietnam drug addiction?' (American Journal of Public Health, supplement 64), the source cited for the 5% first-year figure (p. 1045); no project record.

Robins, Helzer and Davis, interview study of 898 Vietnam returnees (Archives of General Psychiatry), one of the study's primary reports, listed in this lecture's bibliography (p. 1054); has a project card.

Robins, Helzer, Hesselbrock and Wish, 'Vietnam veterans three years after Vietnam' (book chapter), cited for the 3-year results such as half of the men who used heroin regularly being re-addicted (p. 1046); no project record.

Heyman's review cites this lecture for treated and untreated veterans' relapse (6% treated; nearly 70% against under 12%) and for remission of 95%, 88% and 96% at 1, 3 and 24 years, the last from a 1996 follow-up (Ledgerwood et al., 2008; Price et al., 2009); its restatement mixes the lecture's denominators (see sc_heyman_2013).

replication.where_it_stands: The Vietnam follow-up remains the main population-based evidence that heroin addiction acquired in one setting often ends after the setting changes, mostly without treatment. Its primary reports (Robins, Helzer & Davis, 1975, with a project card; Robins, Davis & Nurco, 1974; Robins et al., 1980) hold the methods and denominators this lecture omits; a 1996 follow-up of the same men is described only second-hand in the project's files (Heyman, 2013, pp. 44–47). Its generalization to people who become addicted in ordinary civilian life, with the usual risk factors, is argued rather than shown.

funding.funder: The study was funded through the National Institute of Mental Health, the Department of Defense, the Veterans Administration and the Department of Labor, brought together by Dr Jerome Jaffe of the White House Special Action Office for Drug Abuse Prevention (p. 1043). No funding statement for the lecture itself.
funding.affiliations_note: Lee N. Robins, Department of Psychiatry, Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis (p. 1041). The author notes that the Department of Defense was pleased with the findings and insisted on sponsoring the press conference that announced the first results, which may have fed suspicion of a whitewash; a New York Times reporter's investigation did not support that suspicion (pp. 1047–1048). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective population study of people who develop opioid dependence in ordinary civilian settings, with the usual risk factors, followed with repeated diagnostic interviews and biological tests through changes of setting (or none), recording treatment and its timing, to estimate remission and re-addiction with confidence intervals and to test whether setting, treatment or severity explains them.

domains.note: The six supporting studies were chosen by the author; no search or criteria.
Some limits are named (Winick could not show that people had stopped; most ECA cases did not involve heroin), others are not; the study's own figures are not given with denominators or intervals.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The lecture reviews the author's own study; of the other studies it cites in support, two are hers (the St Louis study and the ECA).
Opinions are marked as the author's ('I think', 'I am unrepentant'), and the idea of a biological vulnerability to re-addiction is offered as unknown (p. 1053).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether rapid recovery generalizes beyond Vietnam
domains.note: Three counter-arguments (a whitewash, war stress, change of setting) are stated and answered, but mainly with data from the same cohort; the author's own caution that the Vietnam situation was unprecedented sits beside the claim that the results were not unique.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a lecture reviewing the author's own study (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the worst domain. The figures are first-hand from the principal investigator, but methods are given only in outline, most percentages lack denominators and intervals, and several text figures differ from the lecture's own graphs. Cite the primary reports for numbers where possible; cite this lecture for the 3-year re-addiction figure, the treatment findings and the author's interpretation, with her own caveat about Vietnam's unusual conditions.

key_findings.finding: Sampling: US Army enlisted men who left Vietnam in September 1971, drawn from the active-duty roster and, to over-sample men who used heroin, from the Surgeon General's records of positive departure urines (weighted back to the population); draft-eligible civilians matched on age, region and education served as comparison. Interview completion was 96% at 8–12 months after return, and 94% of those were re-interviewed at 3 years; 97% of men whose military record showed narcotic use reported it.
key_findings.locator: Why the study was a technical success, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1042, right column); The study's assets, (B) and (C) (p. 1043, left column)

key_findings.finding: Almost half (45%) of Army enlisted men in Vietnam in 1970–71 tried narcotics: 34% tried heroin and 38% opium; close to 80% used marijuana, and marijuana and narcotic use were distinctively greater than in the civilian comparison sample.
key_findings.locator: The major findings, (1), 1st paragraph (p. 1044, left column) and 4th paragraph (p. 1044, right column, continuing on p. 1045); Figure 1 (p. 1044)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (percent using at all) shows about 93% alcohol, 75% marijuana, 40% opium, 36% heroin, 25% amphetamines and 24% barbiturates (read from the figure; denominator not stated).

key_findings.finding: Twenty per cent said that in Vietnam they had felt strung out or addicted to narcotics; nearly all of them had used heavily for a considerable time and had classic withdrawal for at least several days, so the authors accepted the claims. Almost 11% of enlisted men's urines were positive at departure; if the screen caught only men who could not stop when warned, about 1,400 recently or still addicted enlisted men were arriving in the US each month.
key_findings.locator: The major findings, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: Why use was so common: heroin in Vietnam was cheap (about $6 a day for a man who was addicted), pure and did not have to be injected; more than 80% of men were offered it, usually within a week of arrival; men who became addicted typically began early in their tour, before exposure to combat. Asked why they used narcotics, men volunteered: to feel high 40%, to tolerate Army regulations 13%, to relieve boredom 9%, to relieve depression 9%, to relieve fear 8%, to pass time 5%, to be one of the group 3%.
key_findings.locator: The major findings, 1st paragraph (p. 1044, right column); The response to the study by the DoD, the press, and the research community, rebuttal (2) (p. 1048, right column, continuing on p. 1049); Table 1 (p. 1050)

key_findings.finding: Pre-service history predicted narcotic use in Vietnam: by variety of illicit drugs used before service, 27% (none), 46% (one), 76% (two types), 91% (three) and 100% (four or more) used narcotics in Vietnam; use rose with the score for pre-service deviance (fighting, truancy, drunkenness, arrest, expulsion). Men who saw more combat were not more likely to use once pre-service history was taken into account.
key_findings.locator: The major findings, (3) (p. 1045, left column, continuing in the right column); Figure 3 (p. 1046); The response to the study by the DoD, the press, and the research community, rebuttal (2) and the next paragraph (p. 1049, left column); Figure 7 (p. 1050)
key_findings.note: Figure 3 shows about 21%, 43%, 54% and 79% using narcotics in Vietnam for deviance scores of none or one, two or three, four or five, and six or more (read from the figure).

key_findings.finding: In the first year after return, only 5% of men who had been addicted in Vietnam were addicted in the US (citing Robins, Davis & Nurco, 1974), whereas two-thirds of young men treated at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington were re-addicted within 6 months of release (Stephens & Cottrell, 1972); even veterans still using narcotics at departure were doing very well 8–12 months after return.

Narcotic use in the 8–10 months after return among men first addicted in Vietnam (read from Figure 4): general sample (n=90) about 65% no use, 21% light use, 12% heavy use, 2% addiction; drug-positive sample (n=341) about 61%, 22%, 10% and 7%; 122 NARA patients 6 months after release to aftercare, about 11%, 6%, 14% and 70%. Inset, 106 men with narcotic experience before Vietnam: about 45%, 33%, 10% and 13%.
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi enlargement of the scanned figure; approximate. The use categories are not defined.

key_findings.finding: At the 3-year follow-up, only 12% of men addicted in Vietnam had been addicted at any time since return, and for those re-addicted the addiction had usually been very brief.

Recovery did not require abstinence: nearly half of the men addicted in Vietnam tried narcotics again after return, but only 6% 'overall' were re-addicted; even men who used heroin regularly were re-addicted in only half of cases (citing Robins et al., 1980).
key_findings.locator: The major findings, (4), 3rd paragraph ('Nor did recovery require abstention', left column); Figure 6 (p. 1049)
key_findings.note: Figure 6 shows about 61% of men addicted in Vietnam using narcotics in the US, 43% heroin and 24% regular use, with about 12% re-addicted in each bar (read from the figure); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Re-addiction was usually brief: only one-fourth of men re-addicted by the first interview (8–10 months after return) were addicted at any time in the next 2 years, and few had positive urines at either interview. Figure 8: of men addicted in year 1, about 30% were addicted in years 2–3, about 50% used without addiction and about 20% abstained; of year-1 abstainers, about 12% used and almost none were addicted (read from the figure).
key_findings.locator: The response to the study by the DoD, the press, and the research community, rebuttal (3) (p. 1049, left column, continuing in the right column); Figure 8 (p. 1051)

key_findings.finding: Treatment did not explain the recovery: only a third of men addicted in Vietnam received even simple detoxification in service; after return, less than 2% of men who used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of men positive at departure who kept using entered drug treatment (citing Robins, 1975). Men who did enter treatment relapsed as often as the civilian Lexington patients, two-thirds by the time of interview, often on the day they left hospital.
key_findings.locator: The major findings, (4), 2nd paragraph (p. 1045, right column, continuing on p. 1046); Figure 5 (p. 1048)
key_findings.note: Figure 5 (relapse to drug use after VA in-patient treatment, sample size not stated) shows about 18% relapsed at the first point, 22% by week 1, 33% by week 4, 46% by week 12 and about 72% at the last, unlabelled point (read from the figure).

key_findings.finding: Men who used heroin after return also used many other drugs: more than 80% amphetamines, more than 70% barbiturates, almost all marijuana; more than half of men addicted to heroin named alcohol or marijuana as their main drug. Heroin went with more adverse outcomes (crime, unemployment, divorce or separation, violence, alcohol and drug problems and others) than barbiturates and amphetamines, but not once pre-service behaviour problems and the number of other drug types used were held constant; the variety of drugs predicted adverse outcomes better than which drugs were used.
key_findings.locator: The major findings, (5) and the following paragraph (left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: Among veterans who returned to narcotics, none of the variables that predicted use and addiction in Vietnam predicted who became re-addicted: pre-service behaviour problems; parents' substance use, arrest or psychiatric care; drug use in Vietnam (types, duration, injection); IQ; draftee or volunteer; combat; military discipline problems; demographic characteristics. The author suggests vulnerability to re-addiction may be biological, whether present from birth or created by the drug, and that different factors operate at each transition (to use, to addiction, to remission, to relapse).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Where to the Vietnam study's findings stand now?, last paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Other studies cited as consistent: 50 untreated people free of heroin addiction for at least 2 years had a median addiction of 5.7 years (Waldorf & Biernacki, 1979); among young men 18–28 registered with Selective Service, 13% of those reporting heroin use had been treated, and 27% of the untreated against 65% of the treated had used heroin in the past year (O'Donnell et al., 1976); 25% of Harlem youths aged 18–23 who had used heroin twice or more had used it in the current year, 16% of the untreated (Brunswick, 1979); in the ECA, substance abuse had the shortest mean duration of any psychiatric disorder, 2.7 years, and one in five people dependent on or abusing an illicit drug had been treated, most of them not for heroin (marijuana was the most common drug).
key_findings.locator: Where to the Vietnam study's findings stand now?, items (2), (4), (5) and (7) (p. 1050, continuing on p. 1051)

key_findings.finding: The author concludes the results were correct and not unique, while stating that so many young men had never before been addicted to opiates in the absence of the usual risk factors and that few of the men addicted in Vietnam would have become addicted had they stayed in the US; their brief addiction and spontaneous recovery, and their ability to use again without re-addiction, were out of line only with American beliefs.
key_findings.locator: Where to the Vietnam study's findings stand now?, 1st paragraph after item (7) ('So, I am unrepentant', left column)

key_findings.finding: She draws three implications: addiction looks very different in a general population than in treated cases (people in treatment have special problems that getting them off drugs will not solve); heroin is not an exceptional drug, its link with long-term addiction and crime owing as much to its reputation as to its effects; and most people who use heroin use many substances, yet treatment is organized by drug. In the ECA (early 1980s), people with heroin problems in the past year had a 35% chance of being seen in a drug treatment facility, people with problems with other drugs only less than 2%, and only 0.7% of the population met criteria for opiate abuse or dependence.
key_findings.locator: Where to the Vietnam study's findings stand now?, 2nd to 4th paragraphs after item (7) (p. 1051, continuing on p. 1052); Figure 9 and the 6th paragraph after item (7) (p. 1052)

key_findings.finding: She attributes the veterans' high rate of use to market conditions (high availability of opiates and lack of alternatives), the absence of disapproving family and friends, and service not being seen as part of their real-life career, and states that their readiness to recover did not differ from that of other people who use; the surprise of press and scientists came from expectations based on relapse rates in patient populations.
key_findings.locator: Where to the Vietnam study's findings stand now?, 5th paragraph after item (7) ('As I look back', left column)

key_findings.finding: The expected surge in demand for Veterans Administration treatment from returning men never occurred; a New York Times reporter's two-month investigation did not support suspicion of a Department of Defense whitewash, and the published article barely mentioned the study.
key_findings.locator: The response to the study by the DoD, the press, and the research community, rebuttal (1) and the following paragraph (left and right columns)

reporting_issues.issue: Three re-addiction figures are given: 5% addicted in the first year and 12% at any time in 3 years (p. 1045), and '6% overall' re-addicted (p. 1046), the last citing Figure 6 with no time frame. Figure 6 itself shows about 12% re-addicted, and about 61% of men addicted in Vietnam using narcotics and 43% using heroin in the US (read from the figure), against the text's 'nearly half' who tried narcotics again.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 5% (first year) and 12% (3 years) with their stated time frames; the 6% has no stated basis, and Figure 6 matches the 3-year 12%.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says one-fourth of men re-addicted by the first interview were addicted at any time in the next 2 years (p. 1049); Figure 8 appears to show about 30% (read from the figure).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 'about a quarter to a third' is what the lecture supports.

reporting_issues.issue: The first interview is dated 8–12 months after return in the text (pp. 1042, 1045) and 8–10 months in the Figure 4 caption and on p. 1049.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; state the first follow-up as 8 to 12 months after return.

reporting_issues.issue: The 5% first-year figure lies between the values read from Figure 4 for men first addicted in Vietnam in the general sample (about 2%) and in the drug-positive sample (about 7%); how the samples were combined or weighted is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 5% is presumably a weighted estimate; its precision cannot be judged from the lecture.

reporting_issues.issue: No total sample size is given in the text: the only counts are in Figure 4 (90, 341 and 106), the statement that over 600 men who used narcotics in Vietnam were interviewed (p. 1043), and reference titles naming 898 returnees (pp. 1053–1054); 'addiction' is not defined beyond the self-report check (p. 1044).
reporting_issues.consequence: Denominators and definitions must be taken from the primary reports (for example robins_1975).

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 values (marijuana about 75%, opium about 40%, heroin about 36%; read from the figure) differ slightly from the text on the same page (close to 80%, 38% and 34%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; perhaps unweighted against weighted figures, which the lecture does not say. Cite the text values.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says people with problems with other drugs only were only a little less likely than those with heroin problems to receive some kind of psychiatric care (p. 1051), but Figure 9 appears to show about 29% against 43% for other care alone, and about 2% against 34% in a drug facility (read from the figure).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the Vietnam findings; the ECA treatment comparison should be cited from its primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: The treatment figures (less than 2%, 6% and 14% entering treatment after return) cite 'Robins, 1975', which the bibliography lists as a Veterans Administration conference highlight, not the Archives of General Psychiatry paper (Robins, Helzer & Davis, 1975) (pp. 1045–1046, 1053).
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary source of the treatment figures is a conference report that is hard to check; the lecture is the accessible source.

reporting_issues.issue: The matched civilian comparison group is described (p. 1042), but none of its figures are given; the only comparative statement is that marijuana and narcotic use were distinctively greater in the veterans (pp. 1044–1045).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lecture cannot be cited for numerical differences between veterans and civilians.

verification.source_read: PDF (scan of the printed version of record), Addiction 88, pp. 1041–1054 (all pages; the text layer is a poor OCR, so every number was read on the rendered pages; Figures 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 enlarged at 300 dpi; values marked as read from a figure are approximate; the last PDF page is the scanning service's disclaimer; no supplement). Paragraphs are counted within each printed heading; in 'The major findings' and 'Where to the Vietnam study's findings stand now?' the author's numbered items are used as locators.
